name: Flying Cars Parallel
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Where Is My Flying Car
lesson.summary: Flying cars have actually been built, repeatedly, for close to a century, yet the mass market version never arrives, a different flavor of the 40 Years of Promises pattern driven by deployment barriers rather than unsolved science.
lesson.body:
"Where is my flying car" has become a stock phrase for expressing disappointment that the future did not arrive on schedule, and it captures a slightly different flavor of the 40 Years of Promises pattern than fusion energy does. Flying cars have actually been built, repeatedly, for close to a century. Working prototypes existed in the 1940s. More have been built in nearly every decade since, including flight capable, road legal vehicles and electric vertical takeoff aircraft in recent years. The core engineering problem, a vehicle that can both fly and drive, or fly affordably and safely for ordinary operators, has been solved in the narrow sense of "it has been done" many times over.

What has never arrived is the version that was actually promised: flying cars as a normal, mass market mode of everyday transportation, available to typical commuters the way an automobile is. That gap has persisted not primarily because of some remaining scientific mystery, but because of an accumulation of unglamorous, non scientific constraints: airspace regulation, noise, the training required to safely pilot an aircraft compared to driving a car, the cost of manufacturing and insuring something far more complex than a ground vehicle, and the difficulty of many untrained operators sharing crowded airspace without a rise in accidents.

This is a useful complement to the fusion parallel because it highlights a different failure mode. Fusion has not delivered because the physics and engineering are still genuinely unsolved at commercial scale. Flying cars have not delivered even though a version of the core technology clearly works, because deployment at scale runs into a web of practical, regulatory, and economic barriers that a demo flight, however impressive, does not touch at all. Quantum computing coverage often blurs exactly this distinction: a demonstration that an algorithm works on one piece of hardware in a lab gets reported as though it settles whether the technology will be commercially useful, when the gap between working once under controlled conditions and being reliable, affordable, and widely deployed can be as large as the gap between a 1940s prototype flying car and one in every driveway.

There is also a selection effect worth noticing in both cases. The prototypes that get photographed and covered by the press are, understandably, the impressive ones: the smoothest flight, the cleanest quantum algorithm run, the result chosen because it worked well rather than because it was representative of the technology's typical, current reliability. A reader who only sees the highlight reel, whether of flying car test flights or of quantum processor demonstrations, naturally overestimates how close the ordinary, everyday version of the technology is, because that version is defined by its worst days and unglamorous constraints, and those rarely make the news.

The lesson to carry forward is that "the core technology has been demonstrated" and "this will be available to me in some affordable, reliable form soon" are two separate claims, and quantum computing coverage, like flying car coverage before it, tends to treat the first as though it implies the second. It does not. Between a working lab demonstration and a widely deployed technology sits an enormous amount of unglamorous engineering, cost reduction, and reliability work a single headline never captures, and that gap is exactly where earlier patterns in this guide, moving goalposts, unfalsifiable timelines, and redefined success, do their quiet work.
